name: The Tomb of Gül Baba
description: The Tomb of Gül Baba is an octagonal Ottoman tomb on Rózsadomb, built between 1543 and 1548 for a Bektashi dervish who died in 1541. It later served as a Jesuit chapel, was restored several times, and is described as the northernmost Islamic pilgrimage site in the world.

children.text: The Tomb of Gül Baba is an octagonal Ottoman tomb on Mecset Street in the Rózsadomb district of Buda, a short but steep walk from Margaret Bridge. It was built between 1543 and 1548 on the orders of the Ottoman pasha of Buda, and has a shallow dome covered with lead plates and wooden tiles. Wikipedia describes it as the northernmost Islamic pilgrimage site in the world.

Gül Baba was a Bektashi dervish and poet, and a companion of Sultan Suleiman I. He is thought to have died in 1541 around the time of the Ottoman capture of Buda; accounts differ on whether he died during the first Muslim religious ceremony in the city after the victory or was killed fighting beneath the city walls. Suleiman is said to have declared him patron saint of the city. In Hungary he is known as the Father of Roses, which Wikipedia calls a probable misunderstanding of the mystical meaning of his name, noting that roses were already in Hungary before the Ottoman conquest.

The tomb survived the Habsburg capture of the area in 1686, after which the Jesuits turned it into a Roman Catholic chapel dedicated to St Joseph. Later, János Wagner owned the land, maintained the site and allowed Muslim pilgrims from the Ottoman Empire to visit. In 1885 the Ottoman government commissioned a Hungarian engineer to restore it; the work was completed in 1914, and the tomb was declared a national monument.

The tomb was restored again in the 1960s and the 1990s. A large renovation was completed in October 2018, and the site was inaugurated by Viktor Orbán and Recep Tayyip Erdoğan. A 1987 plan by the Hungarian and Turkish governments to build an Islamic centre and mosque there was halted by the political changes of 1989 and nothing was built.
Good to know
Mecset Street, where the tomb stands, is a short but steep walk from Margaret Bridge, so wear comfortable shoes.
Check the official site or Budapest Info for current visiting arrangements, as access to the tomb and its grounds may be limited.
It is a religious and pilgrimage site for some visitors, so dress and behave respectfully.

historyIntro: The tomb of Gül Baba is a small domed Ottoman shrine on Rózsadomb, described as the northernmost Islamic pilgrimage site in the world.

children.text: Gül Baba was a member of the Bektashi dervish order who died in Ottoman Buda in 1541. His tomb (türbe) was built between 1543 and 1548 by Mehmed Paşa, the beylerbeyi of Buda; it is octagonal with a shallow dome. The tomb became an important pilgrimage site, and the Ottoman traveller Evliya Çelebi reported that more than 200,000 Muslims attended his funeral prayer.

historySections.heading: A chapel, then a national monument

children.text: The tomb was not damaged when Habsburg armies took Buda in 1686, and the Jesuits later converted it into a Roman Catholic chapel dedicated to St Joseph. In 1885 the Ottoman government commissioned a Hungarian engineer to restore it; the work was completed in 1914 and the site was declared a national monument. It was restored again in the 1960s and, according to the cited article, in 2018. The tomb stands on Mecset (Mosque) Street in the Rózsadomb district, a short but steep walk from Margaret Bridge.

stories.title: The Father of Roses and the name Rose Hill

children.text: Gül Baba's name is often rendered as 'Father of Roses'. A local tradition connects him with extensive rose gardens on the hillside and says that Rózsadomb, or Rose Hill, received its name from him.
The picturesque story is part of the site's traditional identity; the direct origin of the district name should not be treated as an independently proven fact.

stories.sourceLabel: Visit Hungary — Gül Baba and Rose Hill tradition

stories.title: A funeral attended by a sultan?

children.text: A story associated with Gül Baba says that Sultan Suleiman I personally attended a magnificent funeral following the taking of Buda in 1541.
The account is presented as a legend in descriptions of the monument, not as a confirmed historical detail.

name: Café Gerbeaud
description: A confectionery founded in 1858 that moved to Vörösmarty Square in 1870 and took its name from the Swiss-born confectioner Emil Gerbeaud. Marble, exotic woods and Rococo-style stucco shaped the interior, and the café survived nationalisation under another name before the Gerbeaud name returned in 1984.

children.text: Café Gerbeaud stands on Vörösmarty Square in downtown Pest and is one of the best-known coffeehouses in Budapest. Gerbeaud's own timeline says the confectioner Henrik Kugler opened a café-confectionery on 14 October 1858 at what is now József nádor Square, and that he moved to today's Vörösmarty Square in 1870. Wikipedia says the new premises were on the ground floor of the head office of the Hungarian Commercial Bank of Pest, when the square was still called Gizella Square.

The name comes from Emil Gerbeaud, a Swiss confectioner who gained experience in Germany, France and England. Kugler had no successor and met Gerbeaud in Paris in 1882. Gerbeaud came to Budapest as a partner, gradually took over the shop and kept the original name. He introduced products such as butter creams, Parisian creams and many tea pastries. Wikipedia reports that by the end of 1899 he employed about 150 people, and Gerbeaud's own timeline notes that he served on the juries of world fairs in Brussels and Paris and received the French Legion of Honour.

The interior owes much to a 1910 design with advice from Henrik Darilek, who mainly used marble, exotic woods and bronze, according to Wikipedia. The ceiling stucco is in the Rococo style of Louis XV, the chandeliers were inspired by Empress Maria Theresa, and the café had French and Secessionist tables bought at the Paris world fair. Wikipedia lists Ferenc Deák, Franz Liszt and Empress Elisabeth among its guests.

Emil Gerbeaud died on 8 November 1919 and his wife ran the business until 1940. The shop was nationalised in 1948 and renamed Vörösmarty after the poet Mihály Vörösmarty, and the Gerbeaud name returned in 1984. In 1995 a German businessman, Erwin Müller, bought the building, according to the café's timeline, and the interior and offer have been renewed since, most recently in 2025. Váci utca, the pedestrian shopping street, begins at the square, and the Vörösmarty tér station of the M1 metro lies beneath it.
Good to know
The M1 metro runs under Vörösmarty Square, and Váci utca, the pedestrian shopping street, starts at the square.
Sources disagree on small details, such as whether Gerbeaud arrived in 1884 or a year after meeting Kugler in 1882, so treat exact early dates with care.
Check the official site for current opening times and the seasonal terrace arrangements before you go.

historyIntro: Café Gerbeaud is one of the places where Budapest's tradition of elaborate confectionery meets the social history of its grand city-centre cafés.

historySections.heading: From Henrik Kugler to Emil Gerbeaud

children.text: Confectioner Henrik Kugler opened a café in Pest in 1858, moving to the square now known as Vörösmarty Square in 1870. The Swiss-born Emil Gerbeaud joined the business in the 1880s and helped turn it into an internationally known name in cakes and chocolates.

The business survived war and changes in ownership. After post-war nationalisation, the café operated under the name Vörösmarty before the historic Gerbeaud name returned in 1984. Its continued presence on the square makes it a living part of Budapest's pastry history.

stories.title: From paper cake trays to chocolate classics

children.text: The confectionery's own chronology credits Kugler with popularising cakes sold on paper trays and Gerbeaud with developing an expansive range of sweets. Its history also describes the introduction of cat's-tongue chocolates and cognac sour cherries to the local confectionery tradition.

name: Metropolitan Ervin Szabó Library
description: The central building of Budapest's public library network is housed in the Wenckheim Palace, a neo-Baroque palace completed in 1889. Its ceremonial rooms, including a glass-roofed Imperial Staircase, the Golden and Silver Salons and two ballrooms, are preserved within a working library of more than 1.1 million volumes.

children.text: The Fővárosi Szabó Ervin Könyvtár, the Metropolitan Ervin Szabó Library, is the largest library network in Budapest. Its central library is in the Wenckheim Palace, and the library's own page counts this among the most beautiful palaces of its time. The building is also a working library: it has about 13,000 square metres of floor area, seats 1,000 readers and holds more than 1.1 million volumes, which Wikipedia calls the largest public book collection in the city.

The palace was built when the district behind the National Museum was being laid out in the 1860s and later. Count Frigyes Wenckheim commissioned it, and the Saxon architect Artúr Meinig designed it in a mainly neo-Baroque style with some neo-Renaissance elements; it was completed in 1889. According to the library, the family kept the palace for only about 15 years after the count's death. In 1919 it was expropriated, first for a joiners' craft association and then for the Proletarian Museum, and it was briefly occupied by the Romanian army that year. Political parties and a journalists' and artists' club used it afterwards.

The library itself was founded in 1904 and was first housed in the Central Town Hall. The capital bought the Wenckheim Palace in 1927, converted it over four years, and the library opened there on 21 April 1931. Because of its architecture the palace could only partly function as a library and could no longer house the growing collection, so the municipal assembly approved an extension and reconstruction in 1997. Work began in 1998 to the design of Péter Hegedűs, and the complex reopened to readers on 12 September 2001. In 2003 it received the Prix d'Excellence of the International Real Estate Federation.

The ceremonial rooms are the reason many visitors come. A wrought-iron triumphal arch at the Szabó Ervin tér entrance leads to the Imperial Staircase, which has stucco ornament and marble and is lit through a glass roof. From the oval Reception Hall, which has fireplaces on both sides, the Golden Salon and the Silver Salon open off, and a Small and a Big Ballroom are separated by a glass door, with an orchestral gallery above and large mirrors facing the windows. The Mirrors' Corridor was originally a resting place for dancers. The former Baroque courtyard is now a glass-roofed atrium, and the former stable houses a coffee shop.
Good to know
The library is at Szabó Ervin tér, with the Reception Hall windows facing Kálvin tér, close to the Hungarian National Museum.
It is first of all a working library, so confirm on the official fszek.hu site which areas visitors can enter and when.
The ceremonial halls are used for events, so access to them can vary from day to day.
If you only want to see the interiors, check the library's pages for any guided tours or events before you go.

historyIntro: The central Ervin Szabó Library is an unusual Budapest treasure: a public library whose reading rooms occupy a former aristocratic palace.

children.text: The neo-Baroque Wenckheim Palace was completed in 1889 to plans by Artúr Meinig. Its ceremonial rooms and lavish decoration reflect the social world of an affluent Budapest family at the end of the nineteenth century.

historySections.heading: A palace becomes a public library

children.text: The Central Library moved into the historic building in 1931. Restoration and expansion, completed in 2001, added a new building on Baross utca and renewed the small palace on Reviczky utca, forming one library complex around the palace while preserving elaborate interior rooms, transforming private grandeur into a public place of reading and research.

name: Museum of Ethnography
description: Hungary's museum of ethnography moved in 2022 into a new building at the edge of City Park, designed by Marcel Ferencz of NAPUR Architect. It has a planted roof garden and a facade that carries almost half a million pixels, and below ground there are nearly 7,000 square metres of exhibition space.

children.text: The Museum of Ethnography began in 1872 as the Ethnographic Department of the Hungarian National Museum, and its first director was John Xantus de Vesey. According to the museum's own history page, it became independent of the Hungarian National Museum in 1947. For most of its history it lacked a purpose-built home. Wikipedia lists a series of moves, starting with the Várkert Bazár in 1892 and a building on Csillag utca in 1893, where the first permanent exhibition opened in 1898. In 1906 the collection moved to the empty Hall of Industry from the Millennial Exhibition, and in 1929 it reopened on Könyves Kálmán körút after storm damage. In 1975 it moved to the Palace of Justice opposite the Parliament.

The new building is in City Park at Dózsa György út 35, as part of the Liget Budapest project. Marcel Ferencz of NAPUR Architect designed it, and the inauguration ceremony was held on 22 May 2022, with visitors admitted from the afternoon of 23 May. The museum's director said the opening paid off a debt of 150 years.

The building curves with two wings that carry a roof garden planted with shrubs and perennials, rising to the height of the surrounding trees. The glass facade is covered by a metal grid holding almost half a million pixels that display selected motifs from the collections. Below ground there is almost 7,000 square metres of space for temporary and permanent exhibitions, including a ceramics space where almost 4,000 objects line both sides of a 40-metre staircase. Above ground are a bookshop, a restaurant, a library, a documentation centre and an interactive museum for children.

The collections are among the largest of their kind in Hungary. Wikipedia lists approximate figures including around 50,000 textile and costume items, almost 30,000 ceramic objects, 340,000 photographs, 30,000 manuscripts and 4,500 phonograph cylinders, among them sound recordings contributed by Béla Bartók and László Lajtha. Holdings cover Africa, Asia, Oceania, Indonesia, Europe and the Americas.
Good to know
The museum is at the entrance to City Park, at Dózsa György út 35, close to Heroes' Square and the Kunsthalle at number 37.
Check the museum's official site for current opening times, tickets and which permanent and temporary exhibitions are on.
Much of the exhibition space is below ground, so look at the site's accessibility information if you need step-free routes.
The roof garden is part of the architecture; check the official site for any access arrangements.

heroImage.alt: The dark, angular new building of the Museum of Ethnography in City Park

historyIntro: The Museum of Ethnography explores how everyday objects, dress, ritual and craft reveal the lives of communities in Hungary and beyond.

historySections.heading: Collecting the stories of daily life

children.text: The museum's long history grew from the idea that folk traditions and material culture deserved the same serious attention as royal collections and fine art. Ethnographic research records both continuities and changes in people's lives.

historySections.heading: A contemporary home at City Park

children.text: The museum's modern building beside Városliget gave the collections a new architectural setting. Its exhibitions connect historic objects to contemporary questions about identity and cultural exchange rather than presenting traditions as frozen in time.
